prompt: Two users edit the same shopping cart on different replicas at the same moment: one adds a book, the other adds a pen. The store uses **last-write-wins**. What happens?

options.text: One of the additions is silently lost.
options.explanation: Correct. Each write replaces the whole cart; the one with the lower timestamp is discarded, even though both clients were told their write succeeded.
Wrong. LWW keeps one whole value (the one with the higher timestamp) and discards the other; it doesn't merge.

options.text: Both writes fail with a conflict error.
options.explanation: Wrong. LWW never reports conflicts; it resolves them automatically by timestamp. That's its appeal and its danger.

options.text: The store keeps both carts as siblings.
options.explanation: Wrong. Keeping siblings is what version-vector stores like Riak do; LWW throws one away.

workedExample:
1. Replica A: cart = [book], ts = 10.050.
2. Replica B: cart = [pen], ts = 10.020.
3. Replication: both see both versions; LWW keeps max ts → [book].
4. The pen is gone, and neither user was told.

Better: model the cart as an OR-Set CRDT so the merge is [book, pen].

prompt: A Riak bucket has siblings enabled (`allow_mult`). A read returns two conflicting cart versions. The client merges the carts and writes the result back. The next read contains an additional sibling instead of one resolved value. Which client mistake can explain this?

options.text: Siblings always persist until background anti-entropy runs.
options.explanation: Wrong. A write whose version dominates the siblings makes them obsolete immediately; anti-entropy is not needed to collapse them.

options.text: The client returned the full causal context from its read with the merged value.
options.explanation: Wrong. Returning that context is the correct procedure: it tells Riak which siblings the new write has reconciled. Assuming no new concurrent update, the merged version can supersede them.

options.text: Version vectors cannot describe a merged value, so Riak needs last-write-wins for carts.
options.explanation: Wrong. Dominating both siblings is exactly how a version vector records a merge. LWW would make things worse by discarding one cart's items.

options.text: The client omitted the causal context from its read, so Riak could not tell which siblings it had reconciled.
options.explanation: Correct. A write without context can be treated as concurrent with existing values and create more siblings. The precise sibling count and metadata depend on Riak settings, version and concurrent activity.

workedExample:
The client must communicate both the merged data and what it has seen.

1. In an illustrative version-vector model, merging {A:2, B:1} and {A:1, B:2} takes the entry-wise maximum {A:2, B:2}.
2. If the new update is coordinated by B, incrementing B produces {A:2, B:3}, which dominates both inputs.
3. Riak clients return the causal context received with their read; they should not manufacture that context from cart contents. Without it, Riak may retain the new value as another sibling.

The vector calculation illustrates the ordering rule, not an exact prediction of Riak metadata. Repeated context-free writes can cause sibling explosion.

link.title: Riak conflict resolution and causal context
